pages.text: Wednesday, June 12, 2024 3 More than 50 years ago, KNBR disc jockeys Mike Cleary of Piedmont and Frank Dill challenged their Bay Area listeners to put on a parade, and Pleasanton was selected. It became the KNBR Good Times Parade, and anyone with a little red wagon could enter. A Mariners group at the Pleasanton Presbyterian Church entered with a Viking ship the first year, then came up with the idea of tubby sailors carrying mops. The group quickly became a popular comic marching group. Though many of the men were veterans of various branches of the military, there was a belief that slavish obedience to commands was counterproductive, so the Balloon Platoon was born. Invitations soon came to participate in other communities’ parades. In 22 years, the group has trooped in several bowl games, appeared at the Indianapolis 500 Balloon Platoon returns for 4th of July Parade and marched in the Christmas parade in London. Though not bearing bagpipes the Platoon went to Edinburgh in 2000 to participate in the Millennium Pipe Festival. One spring the Balloon Platoon appeared in the National Cherry Blossom Festival parade in Washington, D.C. The group meets only to decide which parade invitations to accept. “We usually reject offers that are strict forward-motion parades,” explained leader Hal Strunk. “The Marine Corps band does that really well – we do not.” The age of Platoon members ranges from 21 to 80, and all are associated with the church in Pleasanton. As the Balloon Platoon passes by on the 4th of July, look for its special routines: Shake-nBake, pirouettes, carousels, big pinwheels, the Manual of Mops and its famous 21-Mop Salute. The Balloon Platoon, based in Pleasanton, has been a staple of the Piedmont 4th of July Parade for more than 13 years. articles.text: A fire on Wednesday, June 5, totally destroyed the vehicle of a local worker. At around 2 p.m., a domestic worker on Selborne Drive started his car to go home for the day when something malfunctioned and the vehicle caught fire. “Because this was in the middle of the day, and it was a car where the body panels are largely plastic, it created a really large black plume of smoke,” said Dave Brannigan, Chief of the Piedmont Fire Department. “So, we got lots of calls from concerned residents about a fire.” The fire spread quickly and damage to the vehicle was severe. “It was fully engulfed [in flames] by the time we arrived,” said Brannigan. The property on Selborne has a steep driveway which prevented fire engine access to the fire. Firefighters carried their hoses up the driveway by hand to reach the fire. “We had a crew member pretty close to the area, and we got water on it within 10 minutes,” said Brannigan. “The property owners did a great job of having a clear driveway. There was no vegetation hanging down blocking us, nor cars in the driveway, which helps with fire safety, but it also helps us access your property. So, putting your cars in the garage or parking spots and not blocking your driveway is something everybody can do to keep themselves a little bit safer every day,” he said.” For more information, contact the Piedmont Fire Department at 420-3030 or email FireInfo@ piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: California Assemblymember Mia Bonta recently named Children’s Fairyland in Oakland as the 2024 California Non-Profit of the Year. This year marks the ninth year of the California Non-profit of the Year initiative, a state-wide effort honoring nonprofit organizations’ critical role in California. Bonta highlighted Children’s Fairyland’s contributions to young lives in Oakland and across the Bay Area at a ceremony in Sacramento on Wednesday, June 5. Founded on the shores of Oakland’s Lake Merritt in 1950, Children’s Fairyland has served as Oakland’s Storybook Theme Park for over 70 years. The park inspired other cities to open similar storybook parks for children and even inspired Walt Disney’s development of Disneyland. “Children’s Fairyland has long been a center of joy for the East Bay’s youngest residents and an iconic staple of Oakland,” said Bonta. “Annually, the park waives admission costs for over 4,000 low-income children to ensure everyone can experience its attractions. I’m incredibly proud to have this wonderland in my district. It has brought my family’s little ones and so many others a space for their creativity and imagination to thrive. Children’s Fairyland has operated as a non-profit for the past 30 years, and I’m honored to name them Non-Profit of the Year for Assembly District 18 for the continued enjoyment and learning they provide our community.” “We are honored to be recognized as the 2024 California Nonprofit of the Year by Assemblymember Mia Bonta for the magic we have woven into the fabric of Oakland and the Bay Area,” said Kymberly Miller, the executive director at Children’s Fairyland. “Through the unwavering support from our community, we will continue to serve families across the region and keep the tradition of fostering creativity, imagination, storytelling, and a love for learning alive for the next 75 years.” Nearly all of California’s 120 state legislators select their own Non-Profit of the Year as part of California Nonprofits Day. Now in its ninth year, the program seeks to highlight local nonprofits across the state. Since its inception, more than 774 different nonprofit organizations have been selected. Bonta represents California’s 18th Assembly District which includes Oakland, Alameda, Piedmont, and Emeryville. She also chairs the Assembly Health Committee. articles.text: Two fourth grade classes from Beach school collected 101 pounds of trash during their 4th-grade community service field trip on May 24. Students in small groups with parent leaders walked around the neighborhoods of Piedmont and Oakland and collected 6,638 pieces of trash in two hours. The students from the classes of Ben Spencer and Alicia Martinez cataloged every item and then weighed their bags on campus. Last year’s totals, 5,276 pieces and 85 pounds, were significantly outpaced by the students this year. Does this mean they worked harder, or that there is more litter around, students pondered? “Students have been learning about organisms and biomes in science for the last seven weeks,” said Spencer. “Earlier this year we also took a field trip to the Marine Mammal Center in Sausalito. They learned about the impact humans have on our oceans and marine life.” Beach dad Justin Laubach checks the white board and the results of trash collection by each group. Alicia Martinez and Ben Spencer’s 4th grade classes at Beach School show 101 pounds of trash they collected in the school neighborhood. The nine- and ten-year old students were determined to make sure that the trash in their community stays out of storm drains and out of the Bay and the ocean. The field trip engaged students’ minds and bodies by giving them the privilege of getting to be off campus. Parent chaperones took groups to different nearby areas to pick up trash, including the Rose Garden, Piedmont Avenue, Grand Avenue and Dracena Park. Armed with gloves, tongs, and safety goggles the students racked up tally marks on their worksheets showing what’s hiding in bushes and what otherwise would be eventually careening into waterways. One group, in just a couple of hours, collected a dozen medical masks, 50 cigarette butts and hundreds of plastic bottles and plastic pieces. Bottle caps, food wrappers, hair ties, and styrofoam were also easily found in unwanted places around town. The cleanup also functioned as a fundraiser for the Marine Mammal Center, with nearly $700 raised. The center has received tens of thousands of marine mammals since being founded in 1975, namely sea lions, elephant seals, harbor seals, fur seals, and sea otters. articles.text: Dads from Havens, Wildwood and Beach elementary schools battled for bragging rights at Coaches Field on Saturday, June 1, in the annual Buzz Redford Tri-School Softball Tournament. The Wildwood Wild Things took home top honors in the end-ofthe-year round-robin tournament by shutting out both the Havens Dads and the Beach Padres, 4-0, in two seven-inning games. Havens topped Beach 6-2 in the Consolation game, and a team of Alumni tied an all-star team of current players, 7-7. Wild Things manager Alexander Shartsis, a Piedmont native, said the win was big. The last time Wildwood won the tournament was 15 years ago in 2009. That year, the Wildwood pitchers combined for a no-hitter against Beach. The last time Wildwood won a single game in the end of year tournament was 2017 against Havens, when Shartsis was in his rookie year managing the team. The 2024 Wildwood Wild Things brought their gloves and got to work early on Saturday. No runner reached beyond second base in either game. “On defense, John Labrum threw 14 scoreless innings. Randy Wells made at least 12 outs in left field including a slide into the fence on a foul ball that you probably saw on SportsCenter,” said Shartsis. articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco is currently showing Corrine Smith: Silene Capensis in its series of emerging artists. The exhibit is on view now through June 21. Oakland-based artist Smith, who also goes by Critty Smitty, named the exhibition after the Silene capensis root, also known as “African dream.” Her vivid paintings, illustrations, risographs and animations hauntingly capture the artist’s experience with sleep paralysis and night terrors. Smith’s artwork blends the line between reality and fantasy, while displaying a connection to ancestral lineage and eventual healing. The exhibition is presented in conjunction with MoAD’s 2024- 25 emerging artists series, which highlights local, emerging and lesser known artists who work with a variety of mediums. For more information, visit the museum’s website at www. moadsf.org or call 415.358.7200. MoAD is located at 685 Mission Street in San Francisco. Artist Corrine Smith at work

articles.text: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s newest exhibition, Art of Noise, is on view through August 18. It showcases groundbreaking art design that visualizes musical experiences through the decades. Art of Noise features over 800 artworks drawn largely from the SFMOMA collection, including 550 posters, 150 album covers, 100 design objects and four largescale installations that marry design and audio. The exhibition covers more than a century of visual aesthetics from the world of music. “Design has the ability to revolutionize and strengthen our relationship to sound. This unique exhibition shows how trailblazing graphics and design objects fuel our bonds to music and help us develop lasting memories of fleeting musical phenomena,” said Christopher Bedford, a Director of SFMOMA. “Art of Noise also manifests our goal to create captivating exhibitions that connect contemporary culture with art and design from a wide range of makers and perspectives.” Also in the exhibit are music posters by famed artists like Milton Glaser, Victor Moscoso, Bonnie MacLean and Takenobu Igarashi, as well as mid-century modernist record sleeves and album covers by Laini (Sylvia) Abernathy, Emmet McBain, Reid Miles and more. “This exhibition is a chance for visitors to reflect on our collective experience of music as visualized through expressive and often cutting-edge design,” said SFMOMA Associate Curator Joseph Becker. “The San Francisco Bay Area has been an influential center for graphic and industrial design, including audio products that merge aesthetics and engineering, and era-defining posters and fliers. SFMOMA’s design collection reflects these local strengths, as well as iconic designs from around the world, which can be seen in the hundreds of surprising and familiar works on view in Art of Noise.” To purchase tickets and learn more, visit https://www.sfmoma. org.
articles.title: SF MOMA’s Art of Noise exhibition on view through August

articles.text: Asian Art Museum in San Francisco’s exhibition Phoenix Kingdoms, based on recent archaeological discoveries, is on view now through July 22. The exhibition highlights two kingdoms that flourished during China’s Bronze Age, the Zeng and Chu states, encompassing over 2,000 years of imperial history. Phoenix Kingdoms marries art and history while describing one of the most sophisticated, but forgotten, points of Chinese art and culture. The Zeng and Chu states reflect a shamanistic spirituality, rife with belief in human-animal communication, fascination with river and mountain deities, rituals filled with bell and drum music, and a proliferation of magical phoenix totems. “Drawing on the vibrant talent of its artisans and taking advantage of technological advances, the painting, sculpture, calligraphy, and music of this culturally fertile land were developed to an exceptionally high degree,” said Fan Jeremy Zhang, Asian Art Museum’s Curator of Chinese Art. “It was in Chu that a distinctive religious and philosophical tradition evolved and matured into Daoism, a rival to Confucianism that emerged largely in northern China.” “We have no record that speaks of China’s unification from the perspective of the defeated Chu people,” said Jay Xu, Museum Director and CEO. “Because they were never told by the victor, the stories of Phoenix Kingdoms have remained hidden until now.” To learn more, and to purchase tickets, visit https://exhibitions. asianart.org. Museum patrons view artwork in the Phoenix Kingdoms exhibition at the San Francisco Asian Art Museum.
articles.title: Asian Art Museum opens Phoenix Kingdoms exhibit

articles.text: Photo by San Francisco Symphony Four musicians take a bow following San Francisco Symphony’s performance of Schoenberg’s Erwartung. Paying a generous end-of-season dividend, the San Francisco Symphony provided the patrons with a triple bill: Orchestra, a colossal vocal drama and a modern dance troupe, all compressed into a single program. Additionally, the vocal part unleashed the most exciting operatic voice heard all year – Mary Elizabeth Williams acting out the Arnold Schoenberg monodrama Erwartung (Expectation) in passionate, semi-coherent detail. Music director Esa-Pekka Salonen carried off this budget-busting cornucopia of musical treats in the last month of his penultimate season, even as his musicians were leafletting the patrons on arrival about the deficit-plagued orchestra’s belt-tightening moves. These not only led to the announced departure of Salonen, but would also prevent such grand ventures in the future. Clearly, all caution was thrown to the winds with the brilliant modernist Peter Sellars stage-directing Erwartung for the volcanic opera singer Williams, complete with lighting effects and a stage space with a body bag probably containing the cadaver of her lover. She may have been responsible for the latter’s death in her wobbly state of consciousness. The overwrought singer acts out her torments, nebulous frustrations and fears over a searing half-hour span. Written more than a century ago, the halfhour work still packs a hysterical punch, bringing the whole Davies Hall audience to its knees in a unique way. For the most passionate of roles, Williams seems ideally suited, even though her name and her origins in Philadelphia and Iowa would suggest heading in other directions. As an actress, she projects all the dimensions of insecurity, angst, despair and semi-coherent madness, throwing herself about on stage, up and down. Vocally, her voice is a late-romantic volcano of fury, rendering the German poetry unerringly. Projections of English translations of the German were indispensable here. The orchestra was pushed upstage, with conductor Salonen half-turned to enable looking at both orchestra and theatrics. The performance was off the charts. This was a welcome broadening of the performance palette, as only the SFS can afford. It brought in other audiences by offering theater and dance, pairing the Schoenberg with the Alonzo King Ballet doing Ravel’s charming Mother Goose Suite of miniatures. King’s 11-member multi-racial modern ballet company never emulates Mother Goose’s Tom Thumb, Beauty and the Beast or Spinning Wheel. But King, a legend among Bay Area choreographers, finds the languid score a viable backdrop for his designs in movement, which blend ballet and toe shoes with modern dance via his robust, high-quality performers. Originally writing for concert settings, Ravel never introduced a fast-flying allegro segment showing off broader dimensions of dance. But no two works – composed at the same time before World War One – ever reflected better the sharply contrasting concurrent creativity in neighboring France and Germany. MUSIC NOTES Williams is a vocal rarity, singing roles in both the mezzo range (Erwartung) as well as soprano (Wagner’s Isolde). San Francisco Symphony staging both Ravel’s Mother Goose Suite with dancers of the Alonzo King Ballet, and the monodrama Erwartung, June 7-9. For SFS info: (415) 864-6000, or go online, www.sfsymphony.org.
articles.title: French-German opposites at the Symphony

articles.text: Tickets still available for five performances San Francisco Opera’s The Magic Flute, one of the last operas Mozart completed before his death, is being performed at the War Memorial Opera House now through June 30. San Francisco Opera Director Eun Sun Kim teams with producers Barrie Kosky and Suzanne Andrade to bring Mozart’s beloved opera to life, drawing inspiration from the art of silent film, early Hollywood animation and 1920s Berlin cabaret. Kim conducted The Magic Flute with several European companies as well as the Washington National Opera and will now lead the San Francisco Opera’s first presentation in nearly a decade. The cast includes New Zealand-Samoan tenor Amitai Pati as Tamino and Austrian soprano Christina Gansch as Pamina. The international cast also features Estonian bass-baritone Lauri Vasar as Papageno, South Korean bass Kwangchul Youn as Sarastro and Polish soprano Anna Simińska as the Queen of the Night. Sung in German with English supertitles, the opera company has scheduled nine performances: June 14 (7:30 p.m.), 20 (7:30 p.m.), 22 (7:30 p.m.), 26 (7:30 p.m.), 30 (2 p.m.). To purchase tickets, visit www.sfopera.com. The Magic Flute will be performed by San Francisco Opera through June 30.

articles.text: To suggest that Chloe is simply an erotic thriller is to diminish what is an intriguing film. It’s a character study and an examination of a woman’s attempt to bridge what seems an insurmountable distance between herself and her husband. At its center, this is a film not about seduction but about abiding loneliness. It is perhaps best captured by stark scenes where Catherine (Julianne Moore), a successful gynecologist in Toronto, stands looking through windows at the street below at her husband as he sits in his den working on his computer and at her patients in the waiting room. She is suffused with a feeling of disconnection, as if all she has known is now inaccessible and emotionally elusive. She has grown older. She feels less desirable. Her viewpoint has grown clinical. She and her husband, David (Liam Neeson), a professor of music, married some 20 years, have lost contact. She observes him being flirtatious with his students and with other women and suspects that he is having an affair. What she does at this moment, at this intersection in her life, is profoundly human and understandable, yet also immensely destructive. She hires a young prostitute, Chloe (Amanda Seyfried), to test her husband’s fidelity and sets in motion a series of events, in which she insists that Chloe report back the details of her time with David. Unexpectedly, Catherine finds herself in the position of a voyeur, more comfortable with hearing about and imagining the intimacy shared by Chloe and David than searching for a path toward intimacy herself. But then isn’t her voyeurism the handmaiden to pornography (however soft)? Ultimately she finds nothing satisfyingly personal about hearing about David and Chole, and yet she cannot stop herself. She might have hired a private detective, but then perhaps it’s not truth that she is looking for but something else, a fact that Chloe divines from the outset. articles.text: Gary Oldman as Winston Churchill in Darkest Hour Gary Oldman is an essentially unrecognized treasure who represents perfection in his craft, a craft that requires the capacity to inhabit completely another persona. It is truly a remarkable ability. That gift reflects a certain genius. It often requires a disguise, studied mannerisms, facial tics as well as an intimate understanding of who/what one is portraying. And it is that moment when watching Gary Oldman as Winston Churchill that we realize that we are watching an actor in a role like no other. We also quickly come to understand that it is at this moment in the history of England, at the outset of WWII, which is like no other. England had sent the very core of its fighting force (some 300,000) to France to aid in its defense. The German juggernaut has swept across Europe, invading country after country, each falling, one after the other, like so many dominoes. This gesture of assistance to the French resulted in England’s army being pushed by the Nazis and their phalanx of panzers to Dunkirk, the English Chanel acting as a barrier, trapping the soldiers while the German Wehrmacht drew ever closer as their air force strafed the beaches. articles.text: Mission Impossible: Dead Reckoning Part One is the seventh installment of this resilient franchise starring Tom Cruise as Ethan Hunt and his familiar IMF team consisting of Lither Stockwell (Ving Rhames), Benji Dunn (Simon Pegg) and the returning Isla Faust (Rebecca Ferguson). Their mission, should they choose to accept it, is to find a key that will disable an artificial intelligence weapon (referred to as the Entity), capable of destroying all life on the planet. The urgency is, of course, palpable. How this A.I. threat came into existence and who controls it is explained at the outset through long expository meetings between the IMF team. Even if you listen intently, trying to fully grasp the plot, well, it’s a challenge. But then, these frantic, frenetic missions are not about the narrative; rather, what is breathtakingly compelling are the extraordinary risks (stunts) that the M.I. Force takes in order to accomplish their mission, and each iteration proves to be supremely generous in such moments. For example, Ethan, riding a motorcycle drives off a cliff, falling into a 4,000-foot canyon. He is wearing, of course, a parachute. His objective is to land on a runaway train (was it the Orient Express?) racing out of control. Why not simply buy a ticket and board at the station? Well, that’s not entirely clear. But no matter. This stunt is one not to be missed. It’s pure wonder. As is a harrowing ride on the crowded Rome streets in a small yellow Fiat 500 with the Italian police giving chase close behind. This is all while Ethan is handcuffed to the newcomer, the lovely pickpocket (don’t ask) Grace (Haley Atwell). They take turns trying to drive, soon discovering they are also being pursued by what the audience learns later is the White Widow driving a huge, ominous black Hummer which she uses to destroy a remarkable amount of curb-side property while navigating the crowded streets. Outdoor café? Demolished, with people scattering for their lives. Grace, looking back, asks, “Who isn’t chasing us?” And there are more adrenalin-inducing set pieces. Not to forget the runaway train, which Ethan, of course, does land on. The train, absent the disposed of engineers, is approaching a bridge spanning a river far below, where dynamite has been planted at strategic points along its undergirding. The ending is spectacular, astonishing. Forget the plot, ignore the train’s urgent warning whistle. Just enjoy every moment of what is an overthe-top signature Mission Impossible story. The word on the street is that Part Two will arrive next summer. Perhaps. Maybe. The Writers’ strike slowed deadlines just a bit. Lastly, keep in mind that Cruise lobbies to do some of his running, leaping stunt work himself. Yes, he’s 61. When I see him do some of this remarkable stuff, I’m reminded of the movie where, in a diner, a woman watching Meg Ryan simulate an orgasm, says to the waitress, “I’ll have what she’s having.” Ditto, Tom Cruise. Mission Impossible: Dead Reckoning Part One. Directed by Christopher McQuarie. Starring Tom Cruise, Hayley Atwell, Ving Rhanes, Simon Pegg, Rebecca Ferguson. 2 hrs., 43 min. Rated PG-13. They live in New York City and Sherman goes to elementary school. Meanwhile, we soon learn that Sherman and Mr. P. possess what they refer to as the WABAC, a time-travel machine which Mr. P. uses to teach Sherman history. You want to learn about the French Revolution, well, engage the WABAC. At school, Sherman gets into a scuffle with classmate Penny Peterson (Arlei Winter). Mr. P., to make amends to the Petersons, invites the family to dinner. While there, Sherman, breaking a house rule, shows Penny the WABAC and, wanting to impress her, invites her to let him show her how it works. Of course, what can go wrong does go wrong, and they end up creating a tear in the time-space continuum, a ripple of sorts, which has the potential of disrupting world history. Plus, Penny ends up marooned in Egypt while Sherman travels back to the present needing Mr. P.’s help. And thus begins the mission-adventure to rescue Penny.

Wildwood Gardens turns into Woodland Way where Valerie was in her front garden to welcome the group. Initially there was a lawn and few native plants in the Matzgers’ yard, but Valerie learned that three billion North American breeding birds have disappeared since 1970. This population crash is due, among other reasons, to habitat loss, pesticide use, climate change, and predation from cats. Valerie felt we all must include native plants in our gardens to create habitat, eliminate pesticide use, keep our cats indoors, and take action to reduce our contributions to global warming. She installed her garden in stages beginning in 2020, and during the pandemic she transformed her yard. Out went the lawn and most of the non-native ornamentals, and in came a diverse array of keystone species. These are native plants that provide the most value to wildlife. They include holly leaf cherry, California lilac, manzanita, sages, buck wheats, goldenrod, wild rose, lupines, oaks, currants, huckleberries, snowberries, oceanspray, sages, buck wheats, aster, and native strawberries. Dry-stacked moss rock retaining walls were used to create hillside terraces. Valerie led the walkers to the backyard. Flagstone paths took them through the garden with a series of landings and patios. Shady areas were lush with combinations of columbine, ferns, coral bells, and redwood sorrel. There were also California lilac, native fuchsia, and yerba buena on the retaining walls. Scattered throughout the garden were trees and tall shrubs, including coast live oaks, redwood, elderberry, ninebark, toyon, and twinberry. Most of the Scouts came away with stories to tell, including their experience on a rapid called Troublemaker. “Our boat filled up with water and almost capsized. But our amazing guide, Sierra, helped us stay upright and nobody fell out,” said Charlie Parker.
